form.label: Report — Detection Summary
form.description: A plain-language summary of what the detection system looked for and what it found. Written to be read by someone who does not work in security. Export with Export > Export PDF, or schedule it for delivery.

div.div:
Every program that starts on a monitored computer is written down in a log. This system reads those logs continuously and compares them against a public library of known attacker behaviour, maintained by the Sigma project. When something in the logs matches a described behaviour, it is recorded here as a detection.
A detection is not proof of an attack. It is a statement that something happened which looks like a pattern attackers are known to use, and that a person should decide whether it was legitimate. The counts below are grouped so that one piece of activity on one machine counts once, however many log lines it produced.

search.query: | inputlookup sigma_rules.csv | where sigma_technique!="" | stats dc(sigma_technique)
index=sigma_alerts | eval urgency=if(sigma_disposition="immediate","Needs prompt attention","Recorded and watched") | timechart span=1d count by urgency useother=f

panel.title: What was seen, in plain terms

search.query: index=sigma_alerts | stats count as detections, dc(sigma_src_host) as computers by sigma_technique_name, sigma_level | eval meaning=case( sigma_level="critical", "Strongly associated with an active intrusion.", sigma_level="high", "Commonly used by attackers; sometimes used legitimately.", sigma_level="medium", "Can be ordinary activity; worth knowing about in context.", 1==1, "Informational.") | sort - detections | head 12 | table sigma_technique_name, detections, computers, meaning | rename sigma_technique_name as "Attacker technique", detections as "Times seen", computers as "Computers", meaning as "What that means"

| inputlookup sigma_rules.csv | stats count as rules by sigma_platform, sigma_level | eval posture=case( sigma_level="critical","Alerts a person immediately", sigma_level="high","Alerts when the match is specific enough to trust", 1==1,"Recorded and reviewed as a trend") | table sigma_platform, sigma_level, rules, posture | rename sigma_platform as "Operating system", sigma_level as "Seriousness", rules as "Rules in service", posture as "How it is handled" | sort "Operating system", "Seriousness"

index=_internal sourcetype=scheduler savedsearch_name="Sigma Engine*" | stats count as runs, sum(eval(if(status="success",1,0))) as completed, sum(eval(if(log_level="ERROR",1,0))) as failed, latest(_time) as last | eval last=strftime(last,"%F %T"), verdict=case(failed>0,"Some checks are failing — see Engine Health", completed=0,"No checks have run in this period", 1==1,"Running normally") | table verdict, completed, failed, last | rename verdict as "Status", completed as "Checks completed", failed as "Checks failed", last as "Most recent check" | transpose column_name="Item" | rename "row 1" as "Value"

html.div: Detections are produced by comparing logs against the Sigma rule library (sigmahq.io) and are labelled with techniques from the MITRE ATT&CK framework (attack.mitre.org). Neither is specific to this organisation; both are public descriptions of how intrusions tend to work. A count of zero means nothing matched during the period, which is a normal and good result — not that the system was idle. The "Is the system actually running" panel is what distinguishes the two.
